plan.summary: Add a three-level `priority` field to todos end-to-end: shared type + validation in `@todos/shared`, defaulting and partial-update support in the in-memory `TodoStore`, and a priority selector in the React UI (both when creating and when editing an existing todo). Routes need no change beyond what `parse*` already gives them, since validation lives in shared.

ambiguities.detail: The set of priority levels is unspecified — the plan chose three levels (a `Priority` union in `@todos/shared` with a `PRIORITIES` list); the issue never says how many or what they are named.
The default priority for newly created todos is unspecified — the plan invented `DEFAULT_PRIORITY` applied in `TodoStore.create()`.
Whether priority is required or optional on create/update input — the plan made it optional on `CreateTodoInput`/`UpdateTodoInput` to preserve existing callers.

What 'existing todos keep working' means concretely: back-filling already-stored todos that lack a priority vs. only keeping old request shapes valid. The plan interpreted it as request-shape compatibility plus store-level defaulting.
How the UI 'shows' priority — the plan picked a `<select>` per todo plus one on the add form, and added visual emphasis in `styles.css`; the issue only says the important ones should 'stand out'.
Whether 'stand out' implies sorting/filtering by priority, or only visual styling. The plan silently chose styling only, with no ordering change.
Behaviour on an invalid priority value from the API — the plan derived a `parsePriority` returning a 400 `{ error }`, an outcome the issue never states.
Whether priority can be set at creation time at all, or only edited afterwards — the plan supports both.

clarity.rationale: The issue names the feature but fixes no priority levels, default, ordering, or visual treatment, so 'shows it' and 'stand out' are judgment calls; the plan settled every one of those silently and raised no questions.

objections.detail: Step 2 prescribes `(PRIORITIES as readonly string[]).includes(...)` on a parameter typed `unknown`. `Array.prototype.includes` on `readonly string[]` takes a `string`, so passing an `unknown` is a compile error under `strict` (tsconfig.base.json:7), and `.includes()` does not narrow the value to `Priority` either, so the success branch `{ ok: true, value: priority }` needs a cast or a type predicate. As literally written, `pnpm typecheck` fails. The fix is one line — guard `typeof priority !== "string"` first (which also gives a better error for `priority: 3`/`null` than the generic "must be one of ..."), then narrow via `PRIORITIES.includes(priority as Priority)` or a `isPriority()` predicate — but the plan should say so rather than leaving the implementer to rediscover it.

Step 3 test (b) — "omitting priority yields a value with no `priority` key" — does not test what it claims. Vitest's `toEqual` treats `{ title: "x" }` and `{ title: "x", priority: undefined }` as equal (only `toStrictEqual` distinguishes them). Since `parseCreateTodoInput` returning an explicit `priority: undefined` would then be JSON-serialized away by `api.ts`/Fastify anyway, this is mostly cosmetic, but the test as specified is a no-op guard. Use `toStrictEqual`, or assert `"priority" in result.value === false`. Note the file currently uses `toEqual` throughout (packages/shared/src/index.test.ts:6,13,25,31,35), so switching one assertion to `toStrictEqual` is a small, deliberate deviation worth calling out.

CLAUDE.md:45 ("New or changed behavior is covered by a test in the same package") and CLAUDE.md:46-47 ("the API and the UI stay in sync") are both cited by the plan, yet the entire second acceptance criterion — "The UI shows it and lets you change it" — lands in `apps/web/src/App.tsx` with zero automated coverage, verified only by the manual checks. The plan's justification is accurate (vitest.config.ts:5 includes only `*.test.ts`, and apps/web/package.json has no jsdom/@testing-library dependency), and apps/web has no tests today, so this is defensible — but it means the AC that is most likely to regress is the one nothing enforces. If adding `jsdom` + `@testing-library/react` and widening the include glob to `*.test.tsx` is off the table, say explicitly in the PR that this criterion is manually verified only.

Step 6 casts `e.target.value as Priority` in the UI while `parsePriority` stays module-private. That mirrors the existing unexported `parseTitle`, so it is consistent — but CLAUDE.md:34 justifies shared validation as "so the frontend and the API agree on the rules," and here the frontend agrees only by convention (option list generated from `PRIORITIES`) plus an unchecked cast. Exporting `parsePriority` (or a small `isPriority()` predicate, which the parser needs internally anyway per the objection above) would let the select handler narrow instead of assert, at no extra cost.

"So the important ones stand out" (the issue's framing) is carried entirely by `li.priority-high span { font-weight: 600 }`. That competes directly with the existing `li.done span { text-decoration: line-through; opacity: 0.5 }` (apps/web/src/styles.css:72-75) — a done high-priority todo renders as bold-but-faded — and a 600 weight next to the default is a weak signal on its own. Consider a color or a small badge for high, and confirm the interaction with `.done` during the manual pass (the plan's third manual check touches this but only asks that strike-through still works, not that the two styles compose sensibly). Sorting by priority being out of scope is fine; the stated ACs only require show + change.
